submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the words that carry the meaning 'an indeterminate amount of an unbounded substance or abstraction': (a) quantifier/measure/partitive words used over a bare, unindividuated noun - 'much', 'more', 'less', 'little', 'enough', 'some', 'a lot of', 'lots of', 'plenty of', 'amount(s) of', 'quantity of', 'lack of', 'a pinch/cup/spoonful/pound of', 'how much' - which fire on the quantifier itself whatever noun follows, and stand at 2.0-2.9 against 0.1-0.3 for 'many'/'number of' or for a bare comparative ('much taller' 0.15, 'much better' 0.6); (b) the mass/abstract nouns such amounts apply to when they are introduced indefinitely - 'water', 'food', 'work', 'time', 'money', 'evidence', 'research', 'attention', 'damage', 'rain', 'rice', 'salt', 'coffee' - and an attributive modifier standing directly before such an unbounded head ('hard work' 2.5 vs 'a hard chair' 0.0, 'heavy rain' vs 'a heavy box', 'tap/drinking water', 'media/political attention', 'strong growth' 1.4 vs 'strong results' 0.2); the peak is usually on the quantifying or modifying token one to two tokens before the mass noun (and on the mass noun itself when nothing quantifies it, e.g. 'rice' 0.9 in 'the recipe calls for rice'). It is weak or silent on countable, individuated or already-definite referents and on degree-of-a-property uses of the same words ('the water is cold', 'number of cars', 'some of the boys', 'he bought a red car yesterday'), and a second trigger fires on the first, not-yet-resolved piece of an unfamiliar multi-piece word, usually a substance or technical term ('chives', 'leeks', 'gluten', 'salmonella', 'retinopathy', 'whiplash').

adversarial_test_results.prompt: On the first Tuesday of every month the residents of the town gather in the hall beside the old mill. The meeting begins at seven, but people arrive early to talk in the doorway, shaking hands and comparing notes about their gardens. Old Mr Abernathy usually brings a folding chair and sits near the radiator, complaining that the room is never warm. This month the agenda concerned the repair of the bridge at the west end of the high street, which had been closed since the spring. The county engineer had promised a survey in June, then in July, and now in September. Each time the survey was postponed, the minutes recorded a short note and the matter was deferred to the following month. By the time the chairwoman called the meeting to order, every seat was taken and a dozen people stood along the back wall, holding printed copies of the same two page document. The discussion went round in circles for nearly an hour. One speaker argued that the council had already spent a large sum on temporary barriers; another replied that the barriers had been bought second hand from a contractor in the next county and were not fit for the purpose. A third pointed out that the bus route had been diverted through the narrow lanes behind the church, where the hedges scratched the paint of every vehicle that passed. Nobody could agree on who should write to the highways department, or on what the letter should say. At half past eight the chairwoman suggested they break for tea, and the room emptied into the corridor, where an urn had been set up on a trestle table beside a plate of biscuits. There was plenty of time before the next item on the agenda, so the argument resumed in smaller groups, quieter now and harder to follow. When they returned, the secretary read aloud a letter from the department confirming that a surveyor would visit within six weeks. The room fell silent. Mr Abernathy asked whether the six weeks began on the day of the letter or on the day of the visit, and nobody, including the secretary, could answer. The chairwoman said she would write again, and the meeting closed at ten past nine, an hour later than usual, with the bridge still closed and the same two page document folded in a hundred pockets.
